topic: Three numbers on a scrap of paper
text:
Three numbers will tell you more than a month of worrying: what lands in your account each month, what leaves it, and how many months of that you could cover with what you have. That's where I'd start, divorced or not. Write them on a scrap of paper if you have to. The free one-page Three Numbers Starter Sheet at the link in bio gives them a tidier home.

Day one counts.

Boring Money Monday. Open your bank app, scroll back thirty days, and say the total that came in out loud, to the dog if there's a dog. If you're rebuilding after a divorce, that one number is a good place to stand. The free Starter Sheet at the link in bio has a line for it and a line for what went out.

Day one counts.

Here's a question for anyone starting over: if nothing changed at all, how many months could you keep going? Divide what you have by what you spend in a typical month and round it. The answer might be two months or twenty, and either way you finally have a number to work with. The free one-page sheet at the link in bio lays out the math.

Day one counts.

Somewhere in your house there's a drawer or a folder with a year of statements you've been avoiding. Pull out just the most recent one and read what came in and what went out. That covers the first of your three numbers, and it's a gentler start than a full budget when you're rebuilding after a divorce. The free Starter Sheet is at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Most advice for starting over financially opens with what to cut. I like to open with what you keep. Maybe it's the good coffee, a standing lunch with a friend, or the gym that gets you out the door. Protect those first, then look at everything else. What's on your keep list this month?

A plan with no room for joy tends to get dropped by the second month. After a divorce, when everything feels up for review, pick two or three things you're keeping on purpose, like a weekly walk or a pizza night. You made that decision, and you can say so out loud. Which ones are on your list?

Ten-minute exercise for tonight. Write down five things you spend money on that you'd miss badly if they vanished, then circle the two that matter most. Those two get protected first while you rebuild, and everything else can wait for another day. Which two did you circle?

You can want nice things while you're rebuilding. New sheets or a good candle after a divorce is a perfectly reasonable line in a budget when you put it there on purpose. Follow along if you'd like one small money step a day. What's on your keep list?

If money feels tighter than it should after a divorce, look for the small leaks first. A gym you stopped going to, a streaming service nobody watches, a free trial that quietly became a monthly charge. Scroll back one month in your bank app and circle anything you don't recognize. Part 2 of the $17 Day Zero Workbook, Where It Went, walks you through it. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Calling to cancel something or ask for a lower bill is a phone call a lot of people put off for weeks. The Dreaded Call Scripts in the $17 Day Zero Workbook give you words to read out loud while you're on hold. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Autopay is great until you realize you can't name half of what's on it. Take twenty minutes, open a blank page, and list every bill that pulls money out on its own. You might find one to pause. The Year-at-a-Glance Bill Tracker in the $17 Day Zero Workbook gives you a place to keep the list. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

My order is Keep, Cut, Earn, Build, and Cut sits second because the first job is deciding what's worth protecting. After that, trimming feels less like punishment. The whole method is in the 32-page Day Zero Workbook, $17, written for women rebuilding after a divorce. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Think about the last few times someone asked you for help with something: a spreadsheet, a resume, a confusing form. Those requests are a decent clue about what you could offer other people for a fair price someday, and you don't have to quit anything to find out. What do people always ask you for help with?

If all you had was a phone or a laptop, what could you do this month that someone might pay a fair price for? Proofreading, organizing a closet, setting up a friend's budget spreadsheet. Pick one and write it on a sticky note where you'll see it. Follow along if you want one small money step a day. What's your idea?

Before you add any side income, count the hours. Five extra hours a week have to come from somewhere, and after a divorce your calendar may already be full of appointments, errands and sleep you're trying to catch up on. Open your real week and look at it. What would you drop to make room?

Your resume probably undersells you. Writing, organizing, teaching, fixing things, staying calm when a form is due tomorrow: they all count. Write ten skills on a page without editing them, then pick the one you enjoy most. Which one is first on your page?

A good first hour for your money looks something like this: list every account with your name on it, write down each bill and its due date, and change any password you've reused. Nothing glamorous about it, and everything else sits on top of it. Part 4 of the $17 Day Zero Workbook, The First Hour, walks through it. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

When you have fifteen minutes and not much energy, there's a bonus in the $17 Day Zero Workbook called the Fifteen-Minute Start, built for days like that. Rebuilding after a divorce adds up slowly, one finished small thing at a time. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Rebuilding after a divorce feels more doable when each week has one job. Week one, a list of your accounts. Week two, a calendar of your bills. Week three, a small cushion, even if it's twenty dollars. The 32-page Day Zero Workbook, $17, lays out the order. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Before you meet with a lawyer, accountant or planner, it helps to have your questions written down. Questions for a Money Helper is a bonus page in the $17 Day Zero Workbook. A licensed professional can help with the big decisions, and a page of questions gets you in the door prepared. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

It's 2 A.M., you're doing money math in your head, and every number looks worse in the dark. Write the numbers on paper, close the notebook, and look again after coffee. Numbers on paper in the morning often look smaller than the ones in your head at night. Who else has done the 2 A.M. math?

Try asking where did the money go, and open one statement to find out. A highlighter and ten minutes will usually get you most of the way there: circle the three biggest charges, then circle anything you don't recognize. Save this for the next time your brain starts in on why did I let this happen.

Day one counts.

Nobody feels ready to start over with money, and the first week is usually clumsy. Give yourself one small task, like finding the login for your own bank account, and let that be the day. Zero is a starting line. Follow along and we'll keep the steps small. What's your small task this weekend?

Permission slip for this weekend: you may go slowly, you may do a rough first draft of your accounts list, and you may read the same page twice. Starting over at any age, from any place, divorced or not, is allowed to be messy. Send this to a friend who could use it.

Day one counts.

The Monthly Twenty is a standing meeting with your own money: twenty calm minutes, once a month, same chair. Look at your three numbers, see what moved, and pick one small thing for the month ahead. If you're rebuilding after a divorce, it gives the whole project a rhythm. The free Three Numbers Starter Sheet at the link in bio is a handy place to write them.

Day one counts.

A Sunday reset can fit inside one cup of tea. Open your bank app, look at the week, and write down one number you want to remember, maybe what you spent on groceries. Then close the app. The free one-page Three Numbers Starter Sheet is at the link in bio if you'd like somewhere to keep the numbers.

Day one counts.

Once a month, ask three questions: what came in, what went out, and how many months could I keep going if nothing changed? If the answers moved, now you know. If they stayed put, that's useful too. Write them on the free Three Numbers Starter Sheet, at the link in bio, and tuck it in a drawer until next month.

Day one counts.

Put the Monthly Twenty on your calendar like a coffee date with a friend. Same day each month, short agenda, no lecture. Money looks friendlier when you visit it regularly, especially in the year or two after a divorce. The free Starter Sheet makes the visit quick, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.
